title: Accounting Changes, Errors & Subsequent Events
description: Review changes in principles and estimates, error corrections, and subsequent-event treatment.
html:
Why This Topic Is Important

FAR frequently requires you to determine whether an event represents a change in accounting principle, a change in estimate, an error correction, or a subsequent event.

The classification matters because each category can require a different accounting treatment.

The Three Major Categories

ACCOUNTING CHANGE OR ERROR ↓ CHANGE IN PRINCIPLE CHANGE IN ESTIMATE ERROR CORRECTION

Change in Accounting Principle

A change in accounting principle occurs when an entity changes from one generally accepted accounting principle to another generally accepted accounting principle.

EXAMPLE: FIFO → WEIGHTED-AVERAGE

Changes in accounting principle are generally reported through retrospective application, unless it is impracticable to determine the period-specific or cumulative effects.

Retrospective Application

RETROSPECTIVE → PRIOR COMPARATIVE PERIODS ARE PRESENTED AS IF THE NEW PRINCIPLE HAD ALWAYS BEEN USED

The carrying amounts of assets and liabilities may need adjustment, along with the opening balance of retained earnings for the earliest period presented when appropriate.

Example — Change in Principle

A company changes from FIFO to weighted-average inventory accounting.

Assuming retrospective application is practicable, prior comparative financial statements are adjusted to reflect the new accounting principle.

Important Exception — Change to LIFO

A change to LIFO is generally treated differently because reconstructing prior LIFO layers may be impracticable.

CHANGE TO LIFO → GENERALLY PROSPECTIVE

Change in Accounting Estimate

Estimates change because new information becomes available or circumstances change.

These are not corrections of mistakes.

COMMON ESTIMATE CHANGES: USEFUL LIFE RESIDUAL VALUE EXPECTED CREDIT LOSSES WARRANTY OBLIGATIONS OTHER ACCOUNTING ESTIMATES

Prospective Treatment

CHANGE IN ESTIMATE → PROSPECTIVE CURRENT PERIOD AND FUTURE PERIODS AS APPLICABLE

Prior financial statements are not revised simply because management has obtained better information.

Example — Revised Useful Life

Equipment originally cost $100,000, has no residual value, and originally had a 10-year useful life.

After four years, accumulated depreciation is $40,000.

At that point, management estimates that the equipment has 3 years of remaining useful life.

CARRYING AMOUNT = $100,000 − $40,000 = $60,000
NEW ANNUAL DEPRECIATION = $60,000 ÷ 3 = $20,000

The prior four years are not restated. The new estimate is used prospectively.

Change in Estimate Effected by a Change in Principle

Sometimes a change has characteristics of both a principle and an estimate.

A classic example is a change in depreciation method.

CHANGE IN DEPRECIATION METHOD → CHANGE IN ESTIMATE EFFECTED BY A CHANGE IN ACCOUNTING PRINCIPLE → PROSPECTIVE

Error Corrections

An accounting error is different from a change in estimate.

Errors may result from mathematical mistakes, incorrect application of GAAP, or oversight or misuse of facts that existed when the financial statements were prepared.

ERROR → PRIOR-PERIOD CORRECTION NOT A CHANGE IN ESTIMATE

Examples of Errors

EXPENSING AN ASSET THAT SHOULD HAVE BEEN CAPITALIZED FAILING TO RECORD AN ACCRUED LIABILITY MATHEMATICAL ERROR INCORRECT APPLICATION OF AN ACCOUNTING RULE

Prior-Period Adjustments

A material error in previously issued financial statements generally requires correction of the prior-period financial statements presented.

When applicable, the beginning balance of retained earnings of the earliest period presented is adjusted for the cumulative effect relating to periods before those presented.

Example — Prior-Period Error

Assume a company incorrectly expensed $50,000 of equipment in a prior year when the amount should have been capitalized.

This is not a change in estimate. It is an accounting error.

PRIOR-YEAR ERROR → CORRECT PRIOR-PERIOD FINANCIAL STATEMENTS + ADJUST BEGINNING EQUITY WHEN REQUIRED

Estimate Change or Error?

This distinction is heavily tested.

NEW INFORMATION? → USUALLY ESTIMATE CHANGE INFORMATION WAS AVAILABLE BUT ACCOUNTING WAS WRONG? → USUALLY ERROR

Subsequent Events

Subsequent events occur after the balance-sheet date but before the financial statements are issued or are available to be issued, as applicable.

The key question is whether the event provides additional evidence about a condition that already existed at the balance-sheet date.

Recognized Subsequent Events

A recognized subsequent event provides additional evidence about conditions that existed at the balance-sheet date.

CONDITION EXISTED AT BALANCE-SHEET DATE + NEW INFORMATION RECEIVED AFTER YEAR-END → ADJUST FINANCIAL STATEMENTS

Example — Customer Bankruptcy

A major customer was experiencing severe financial difficulty at December 31.

In January, before the financial statements are issued, the customer files for bankruptcy.

If the bankruptcy confirms that the customer's financial deterioration existed at year-end, the receivable and related credit-loss estimate should generally be adjusted.

Nonrecognized Subsequent Events

A nonrecognized subsequent event relates to a condition that arose after the balance-sheet date.

CONDITION AROSE AFTER BALANCE-SHEET DATE → DO NOT ADJUST YEAR-END AMOUNTS

If the event is material, disclosure may still be necessary.

Example — Fire After Year-End

A company's manufacturing facility is destroyed by a fire in January.

The fire was unrelated to any condition existing at December 31.

NO YEAR-END ADJUSTMENT BUT MATERIAL EVENT MAY REQUIRE DISCLOSURE

Subsequent-Event Decision Process

STEP 1 WHAT CONDITION CAUSED THE EVENT? STEP 2 DID THAT CONDITION EXIST AT THE BALANCE-SHEET DATE? YES → GENERALLY RECOGNIZE / ADJUST NO → GENERALLY DO NOT ADJUST STEP 3 IF NOT RECOGNIZED, IS THE EVENT MATERIAL? YES → CONSIDER DISCLOSURE

Example — Lawsuit

A lawsuit concerning an event that occurred before year-end is settled after year-end but before issuance of the financial statements.

The settlement may provide additional evidence about the obligation that existed at year-end.

Therefore, the year-end financial statements may require adjustment.

Integrated Classification Review

CHANGE IN PRINCIPLE → GENERALLY RETROSPECTIVE CHANGE IN ESTIMATE → PROSPECTIVE ERROR CORRECTION → RESTATE / CORRECT PRIOR PERIODS RECOGNIZED SUBSEQUENT EVENT → ADJUST NONRECOGNIZED SUBSEQUENT EVENT → NO ADJUSTMENT POSSIBLE DISCLOSURE

Common FAR Traps

NEW ESTIMATE ≠ ERROR CHANGE IN DEPRECIATION METHOD → PROSPECTIVE EVENT HAPPENED AFTER YEAR-END DOES NOT AUTOMATICALLY MEAN NONRECOGNIZED ASK WHEN THE UNDERLYING CONDITION EXISTED

Key Takeaways

  • Changes in accounting principle are generally applied retrospectively.
  • Changes in accounting estimates are generally applied prospectively.
  • A change in depreciation method is generally treated prospectively as a change in estimate effected by a change in accounting principle.
  • Material errors from prior periods require correction rather than prospective treatment.
  • Recognized subsequent events provide additional evidence about conditions existing at the balance-sheet date.
  • Nonrecognized subsequent events arise from conditions occurring after the balance-sheet date.
  • Material nonrecognized subsequent events may require disclosure even though year-end amounts are not adjusted.

quiz.prompt: After four years of use, a company revises the remaining useful life of equipment based on new information. How should the change generally be accounted for?

choices.text: Restate all prior periods and adjust beginning retained earnings
Record the entire effect as a prior-period error
Apply the new estimate retrospectively from the acquisition date
Apply the revised estimate prospectively to the current and future periods

quiz.explanation: A revision of an asset's useful life based on new information is a change in accounting estimate. Changes in estimates are accounted for prospectively in the period of change and future periods affected by the change.

objectives: Explain accounting changes, errors & subsequent events and its underlying principles.
Apply the topic to a financial-reporting scenario.
